home.title: Home — Haoran Cao
home.subhead: I build small tools, and write down what I learn.
home.intro1: A middle school student from Chengdu, China.
home.intro2: Mostly Swift and SwiftUI, and lately some C#.
home.about.p1: I mostly build for the Mac, because it's what I use every day. Occasionally Windows and the web, too.
home.about.p2: Most of this happens in the evenings and on weekends. I write slowly and try to ship things that feel finished.
project.swiftZip.title: Swift Zip Manager
project.swiftZip.body1: Handles ZIP, TAR, GZ, 7Z, and RAR, including encrypted archives. Browse contents before extracting, drag files from Finder, and pull out individual files without unpacking everything.
project.swiftZip.body2: Built entirely in SwiftUI. Currently in beta, heading toward 1.0.
project.runprocess.title: RunProcess
project.runprocess.body1: A native macOS menu bar app that opens a floating command window on a global hotkey. Real-time output with 8/16/256-color and 24-bit truecolor ANSI rendering, Tab completion for aliases and file paths, frecency-ranked command history with ⌘H fuzzy search, drag-and-drop paths, custom executable paths, and secure sudo handling.
project.runprocess.body2: RunProcess also has a browser demo, hosted on Process WebHub alongside a ProcessSH demo — same interfaces, rebuilt in HTML, CSS, and JavaScript.
project.runprocess.body3: Three appearance modes — None, Frosted Glass, and Liquid Glass (macOS 26+) — let it match the rest of your screen. Session mode keeps a persistent shell alive between launches, so cd and export persist across commands.
project.runprocess.body4: Process WebHub is a static site with working recreations of both desktops: draggable windows, simulated shells, switchable window materials, and custom wallpapers. No install required.
project.processSH.title: ProcessSH
project.processSH.body1: A lightweight Windows app that wraps PowerShell 7 in a Spotlight-style floating window. Opens on a global hotkey, lives in the system tray, and stays out of the taskbar.
project.processSH.body2: Acrylic backdrop, Segoe Fluent Icons, tab completion, command history, drag-and-drop paths, and UAC elevation. English, Simplified Chinese, and Traditional Chinese.
project.processSH.stack: C# · WinUI 3 · Windows App SDK · PowerShell 7
project.taskview.title: TaskView
project.taskview.body1: A native macOS utility for viewing and managing running processes. Reads process information directly from the system using libproc, sysctl, and Darwin APIs.
project.taskview.body2: Process list with PID, name, CPU, and memory. Terminate with SIGTERM or force with SIGKILL. Search, filter, and auto-refresh.
project.fucklang.title: FuckLang
project.fucklang.tagline: A Turing-complete scripting language with an unconventional keyword set.
project.fucklang.body1: A lightweight, cross-platform interpreted language. It strips away unnecessary punctuation, proving that a language doesn't need a massive ecosystem to be fun to write. It supports variables, control flow, first-class functions, and closures.
project.fucklang.body2: Written in Go, it compiles to a single dependency-free binary. It features a multi-line REPL, strict error handling with caret pointing, and a fully automated black-box test suite.
project.fucklang.stack: Go · Pratt parser · Tree-walking evaluator · REPL
project.remotelinkkit.title: RemoteLinkKit
project.remotelinkkit.tagline: WebSocket transport and encrypted framing protocol.
project.remotelinkkit.body1: A Swift package that provides the plumbing for remote command execution. Split into RemoteLinkKit (transport) and RemoteProcessProtocol (encryption and framing), it handles the complexities of Bonjour discovery, heartbeats, and secure channels.

about.title: About — Haoran Cao
about.p1: I'm a middle school student from Chengdu, China. I build small desktop tools to learn — mostly by getting things wrong the first time.
about.p2: I started with SwiftUI because it made a window show up on screen on day one. Everything after that has been one small problem at a time.
about.p3: This site is where I keep the projects I actually finished, and the notes I wrote while finishing them.
detail.runprocess.title: RunProcess — Projects
detail.runprocess.p1: A menu bar app that wraps /bin/zsh in a polished, translucent floating window. Opens on a global hotkey (⌘⌥R by default) and hides automatically when the app loses focus, like Spotlight. Real-time output with full ANSI color support, alias-aware Tab completion, custom paths for running tools and .app bundles by name, frecency-ranked history with ⌘H fuzzy search, multi-line input with Shift+Enter, and secure sudo handling. It also supports App Intents for macOS Shortcuts, custom shells, and Classic/Lite interface modes. Updates ship via Sparkle, and there's a Homebrew tap.
detail.runprocess.note: Requires macOS 12.4 or later · Apple Silicon or Intel · Also on Homebrew
detail.runprocess.p.updates: Updates are delivered through Sparkle and cryptographically signed before installation — check manually with ⌘U or enable daily background checks. Install from the Releases page, or via Homebrew: brew tap CaoHaoran-Dev/apptap, brew trust CaoHaoran-Dev/apptap, brew install runprocess. The app isn't notarized, so the first launch may need Open Anyway in Privacy & Security.
detail.runprocess.p.run: Output streams in real time through Process and Pipe, with ANSI colors rendered properly — git status, ls -G, grep --color all show up as intended. Tab completion covers aliases, command history, system commands, and file paths. History is ranked by frecency (frequency × recency) and searchable with ⌘H fuzzy matching. Aliases let you define short names like gs for git status.
detail.runprocess.p.files: Drag files in from Finder to insert their full paths, properly escaped. Handy for anything that takes a path as an argument. Settings → Paths also lets you add folders like /Applications or ~/bin, so command-line tools found there can be run by name and .app bundles can be launched by name — typing keynote opens Keynote.
detail.runprocess.p.sudo: When a command needs elevated privileges, RunProcess prompts for the password and uses it only in memory during execution. It's never stored or logged — every sudo command asks again. A "Default Sudo" option can lock the main window into run-as-root mode.
detail.runprocess.p.appearance: Three modes — None, Frosted Glass, and Liquid Glass (macOS 26+) — let the window match whatever the rest of your screen is doing. None is a solid system window background. Frosted Glass uses NSVisualEffectView blur and is the default on macOS 15 and earlier. Liquid Glass is the native macOS 26 material, default there and hidden on systems that don't support it. The chosen style applies to the main window, Settings, Help, About, and the sudo dialog.
detail.runprocess.p.interface: In Settings → Appearance, choose between Classic (standard window with output area) and Lite (a minimal, Spotlight-style single-line input that expands only when there is output). Changes take effect in newly opened windows.
detail.runprocess.p.session: By default, each window is its own shell — cd and export are lost after each command. Session mode keeps a long-running zsh process alive within a window, so cd and export persist across commands, closer to a real terminal. It only affects newly opened windows, and the window title shows RunProcess - Session — <current directory>. Multiple windows stay fully isolated from each other.
detail.runprocess.p.intents: RunProcess integrates with macOS Shortcuts and Siri. You can execute commands in the background, search history, add aliases, or clear history using system automations.
detail.runprocess.p.demo: RunProcess is also available in the browser.
detail.processSH.title: ProcessSH — Projects
detail.processSH.p1: A Windows port of RunProcess. A lightweight PowerShell 7 launcher with an acrylic interface, system tray integration, and a global hotkey. Built with C# and WinUI 3.
detail.processSH.p.features: Execute any PowerShell command with real-time output. Tab completion for commands, history, and file paths. Command history with ↑ and ↓. Drag files from Explorer to insert escaped paths. Run as administrator with a UAC prompt.
detail.processSH.p.appearance: Native Windows Acrylic backdrop for a translucent, modern look. The window floats at the bottom-left corner of the screen, inspired by Spotlight on macOS. Segoe Fluent Icons throughout.
detail.processSH.p.hotkey: Ctrl+Alt+R shows or hides the window globally. The default uses Ctrl+Alt instead of Ctrl+Win because Windows reserves many Win key combinations, and RegisterHotKey cannot reliably capture them. Customizable in Settings.
detail.processSH.p.tray: Lives in the system tray, no taskbar icon. Closing the main window hides it rather than exiting. To quit, use Tray → Quit.
detail.processSH.p.lang: English, Simplified Chinese, and Traditional Chinese. Switch at runtime in Settings → Language.
detail.webdemo.title: Process WebHub — Projects
detail.webdemo.tagline: RunProcess and ProcessSH in your browser.
detail.webdemo.p1: A static site with working recreations of both RunProcess and ProcessSH desktops. Draggable windows, simulated shells, switchable window materials, and custom wallpapers. No install required.
detail.webdemo.p.desktop: The demo recreates the desktop environment with draggable windows, a simulated shell, and switchable window materials. It is designed to give you a feel of how the apps work.
detail.webdemo.p.shell: The shell is simulated in JavaScript. It supports basic commands and can be extended to match the actual features of RunProcess and ProcessSH.
detail.webdemo.p.languages: Built with HTML, CSS, and JavaScript. No backend, no frameworks, and no dependencies.
detail.webdemo.p.why: As a way to learn web development and to share the apps with a wider audience. It's a fun side project that complements the native apps.
detail.webdemo.p.limits: It's a simulation, not a full app. Some commands and features from the native apps are not available.
detail.swiftZip.title: Swift Zip Manager — Projects
detail.swiftZip.p1: An archive tool that feels like it belongs on the Mac. Built with Swift and SwiftUI, designed to stay out of the way.
detail.swiftZip.p.formats: ZIP, TAR, GZ, 7Z, and RAR. Encrypted archives are supported. The app checks for the 7zz and RAR command-line tools on first launch and installs them in one click if they're missing.
detail.swiftZip.p.browsing: Open an archive without unpacking it. Contents show up in List or Grid view, whichever suits the archive better. Drag files in from Finder to add them. Extract or delete individual entries without touching the rest.
detail.swiftZip.p.interface: Built entirely in SwiftUI. Native window controls, native menus, native everything. Supports multiple languages. Auto-updates check through the GitHub API.
detail.swiftZip.p.devMode: A hidden mode for the workflows most people never need — the ones I do. Enable it if you know why you'd want it.
detail.taskview.title: TaskView — Projects
detail.taskview.p1: A native macOS utility for viewing and managing running processes. Built with SwiftUI, using libproc, sysctl, and Darwin APIs to read process information directly from the system.
detail.taskview.p.features1: Process list with PID, name, CPU, and memory. Select a process to see details: user, start time, status, path, and parent PID. Terminate with SIGTERM, or force with SIGKILL.
detail.taskview.p.features2: Search and filter to find what you need. Auto-refresh keeps the list current.
detail.taskview.p.issues: This is an alpha. Some user processes show a blank name, and some show Unix Time Zero as their start time. System processes like kernel_task and WindowServer cannot be terminated.
detail.fucklang.title: FuckLang — Projects
detail.fucklang.tagline: A Turing-complete scripting language with an unconventional keyword set.
detail.fucklang.p1: A lightweight, cross-platform interpreted language. The core idea was to prove that a language doesn't need a massive ecosystem or complex syntax to be Turing-complete and fun to write. The interpreter is written in Go, compiling down to a single, dependency-free binary for macOS, Linux, and Windows.
detail.fucklang.p.features: It supports variables, control flow, first-class functions, closures, arrays, and hashes, while stripping away unnecessary punctuation. It includes namespaces for built-ins, assertions with clear abort messages, compound assignment, and comprehensive error handling that reports the exact line number and a caret pointing to the offending source code.
detail.fucklang.p.repl: An interactive shell with multi-line block support (bracket-balanced input), meta-commands, and persistent history. It handles comments gracefully, ensuring that brackets inside comments don't trap the parser.
detail.fucklang.p.testing: The project has two layers of tests: evaluator logic tests and black-box tests that compare byte-for-byte stdout against expected files. GitHub Actions runs the full test suite on Ubuntu, then cross-compiles binaries for x86_64, ARM64, RISC-V, and LoongArch64.
detail.remotelinkkit.title: RemoteLinkKit — Projects
detail.remotelinkkit.tagline: WebSocket transport and encrypted framing protocol.
detail.remotelinkkit.p1: A Swift package that provides the plumbing for remote command execution over WebSocket. It is split into two libraries: RemoteLinkKit (connection, Bonjour, heartbeat) and RemoteProcessProtocol (framing, encryption, message codecs).
detail.remotelinkkit.p.arch: Both libraries are UI-free and execution-free. They do not render ANSI output or spawn processes; those are left to the host application. The transport layer relies on URLSession and Network.framework, while the protocol layer uses CryptoKit for modern cryptography.
detail.remotelinkkit.p.protocol: Every message travels in a frame with a monotonic sequence number. Supported cipher suites include AES-256-GCM and ChaCha20-Poly1305. Session keys are derived per connection using HKDF over client and server nonces, ensuring they are never reused across connections.
detail.remotelinkkit.p.security: The 6-digit pairing code is never transmitted over the wire; it is used as HKDF input and as an HMAC proof. Pairing attempts are rate-limited, and the server only stores token hashes. A ReplayGuard maintains a sliding window of seen sequence numbers to prevent replay attacks.
